title: Preface
summary: Front matter and table of contents of an American Institutes for Research evaluation of remote viewing (Mumford, Rose, Goslin, 1995), prepared for CIA release. Lists chapters: executive summary, background and history, evaluation plan, expert research reviews (Utts and Hyman, with reply and points of agreement/disagreement), utility of remote viewing in intelligence operations, conclusions, and appendices (reviewer vitae, bibliography, interviewer material, StarGate operational tasking evaluation).

title: Executive Summary

nodes.title: Executive Summary (intro)
nodes.summary: Introduces an American Institutes for Research review of a CIA-era remote viewing (paranormal phenomenon) program. The program had basic research, operational applications, and foreign assessment components. The review covered the research program and the remote viewing's intelligence-gathering application; the foreign assessment component was out of scope.

nodes.title: Research Evaluation
nodes.summary: Describes a CIA-released research evaluation of remote viewing. A blue-ribbon panel (parapsychologist Jessica Utts, statistician Ray Hyman, two AIR senior scientists, coordinator Lincoln Moses/David Gostin) reviewed about 80 lab reports. Lab experiments showed statistically significant hits above chance, but causes were unclear: no evidence isolated a paranormal source, and the same judges and target pools confounded effects. Operational evaluation found remote viewing failed in intelligence gathering: conditions differed, reports were vague and inaccurate on specifics, and none were used for actionable intelligence.

nodes.title: Conclusions
nodes.summary: The text concludes that continuing the statistically significant remote viewing program is not justified. Laboratory studies do not show whether paranormal phenomena exist or explain their origins, and methodological issues remain. Even if the effect were real, laboratory conditions have limited applicability to intelligence gathering. Remote viewing targets differ greatly from operational tasks, and the information produced is vague and ambiguous, so it is not useful for intelligence work.

nodes.title: A ERE
nodes.summary: An executive summary concluding that remote viewing, a purported paranormal intelligence-gathering technique, is not useful for intelligence work. Lab results showed some statistically significant effects, but the phenomenon is unproven and lab conditions don't transfer to real operations. End users found the information vague, inconsistent, inaccurate on specifics, and never actionable, so continued program funding is not warranted. Also includes a Chapter One heading on background and history.

summary: An American Institutes for Research review of a CIA-era remote viewing program covering basic research and intelligence applications (foreign assessment out of scope). A blue-ribbon panel reviewed about 80 lab reports: lab experiments showed statistically significant above-chance hits, but no paranormal source was isolated and judge/target confounds remained. Operationally, remote viewing failed for intelligence work: vague, inaccurate, non-actionable reports. Conclusion: continued funding is not justified. Includes a Chapter One background heading.

title: Chapter One: Background and History

nodes.title: Chapter One: Background and History (intro)
nodes.summary: Introduces the background of performance-enhancement research. In the mid-1980s the Army Research Institute asked the National Research Council to evaluate techniques for enhancing human performance; the NAS panel report (1988) found support for some alternatives, such as implicit learning and mental rehearsal, but little for sleep learning, remote viewing, and similar paranormal claims. About 100 later studies on remote viewing were run under government programs, and the CIA took over that program after Congress asked for review. Conducted under AIR direction.

nodes.title: At the request
nodes.summary: Background on government remote viewing research: the 1980s NRC/National Academy review found little support for remote viewing and similar techniques, yet about 100 later studies followed. CIA then commissioned American Institutes for Research (AIR) to evaluate whether remote viewing has practical intelligence value. The text covers the remote viewing paradigm, its statistical and methodological flaws, and the history of DIA's StarGate program (research, operations, foreign assessment) alongside earlier CIA and DIA efforts. It also notes CIA's 1995 declassification and the 1995 ORD contract with AIR for an external technical review with stated objectives.

nodes.title: an evaluation of the overall program utility or usefulness
nodes.summary: An evaluation of the overall utility or usefulness of a CIA parapsychology program, separating scientific validity from operational utility. Covers the review's scope (program results and the DIA/CIA efforts only, not all parapsychology), the two-expert review of research studies, the operational component, and chapter roadmap with recommendations for future strategy.

summary: Background on performance-enhancement and government remote viewing research: a mid-1980s Army Research Institute request led to a 1988 NRC/NAS review finding support for implicit learning and mental rehearsal but not sleep learning or remote viewing. About 100 later studies followed; CIA then commissioned AIR to assess remote viewing's intelligence value, covering the paradigm, methodological flaws, DIA's StarGate history, and CIA's 1995 declassification and ORD contract. The section also scopes an evaluation of scientific validity versus operational utility, a two-expert study review, and recommendations.

Chapter Two: Evaluation Plan (intro)

It outlines the research program's three objectives: establishing the phenomenon's existence, identifying causal mechanisms, and finding techniques to enhance information utility. It reviews the NRC's 1986 assessment and Dr. Edwin May's later studies, then describes a four-member blue-ribbon review panel (Utts, Hyman, Mumford, Rose, plus Moses and Goslin), its review procedures, and resolution of disagreements. Finally, it covers the operational intelligence-gathering program, used by the CIA and DoD from the early 1970s until suspension in spring 1995.

nodes.summary: Describes a CIA remote viewing evaluation plan. Covers expert dialogue on disagreements (Drs. Utts and Hyman, with Dr. Moses), addenda, and the operational intelligence-gathering program (early 1970s to 1995 suspension, used by DoD and agencies). Outlines evaluation methods: prior lab research, interviews with participants, and user feedback analyses, noting limits on operational value of paranormal phenomena.

nodes.title: Prior Research Studies.
nodes.summary: OCR-garbled excerpt from a CIA remote viewing evaluation report (Chapter Two, Evaluation Plan, Approved for Release 2002). Covers: past practice of sending summarized 3-4 page viewing reports to requesting agencies; 1994 formal evaluation of viewer accuracy and value; the need to show a paranormal phenomenon is statistically significant yet operationally useful; multi-source evaluation (prior research, interviews with participants, user feedback analysis); and linking laboratory-established task conditions to operational intelligence requirements, plus the Stargate program and American Institutes for Research.

It also covers analysis of 1994 user accuracy and value ratings (Appendix D), and previews Chapter Three's expert reviews by Drs. Utts and Hyman.

title: Chapter Three: Research Reviews

nodes.title: Chapter Three: Research Reviews (intro)
nodes.summary: Front matter and table of contents of an approved-for-release CIA document (American Institutes for Research) on remote viewing research. Chapter Three covers two expert reviews: Review 1 by Dr. Jessica Utts (UC Davis Statistics, Sept 1995), assessing evidence for psychic functioning; Review 2 by Dr. Ray Hyman; a reply from Utts; points of agreement and disagreement; and conclusions from the expert reviews.

nodes.title: ABSTRACT
nodes.summary: Two-decade government-sponsored research on psychic functioning at SRI International and SAIC is examined to judge whether it is scientifically established and useful for government. The report concludes the effects are well established by standard scientific criteria, replicated across laboratories, and not explained by flaws or fraud. Effect size is small to medium. It recommends future experiments focus on how to use the phenomenon, since further proof-seeking offers little benefit.

nodes.title: 1. INTRODUCTION
nodes.summary: Overview of government-sponsored psychic functioning research, starting early 1970s at SRI (Stanford Research Institute), then SAIC from 1989 under Edwin May. Report examines statistical evidence, methodological concerns, and whether psychic functioning is valid or useful for government purposes. Sections cover SRI program, SAIC work, external validation from other labs, usefulness for government, and conclusions/recommendations.

nodes.title: 2. SCIENCE NOTES
2.1 DEFINITIONS AND RESEARCH PROCEDURES
nodes.summary: Describes ESP types (anomalous cognition: telepathy, clairvoyance, precognition; psychokinesis/anomalous perturbation), noting SRI and SAIC research focused on anomalous cognition via remote viewing, free-response versus forced-choice methods, and difficulty distinguishing telepathy, clairvoyance, and precognition. Also covers statistical issues: human abilities are not reliably replicable on demand, illustrated by baseball hitting analogy.

nodes.title: 2.2 STATISTICAL ISSUES AND DEFINITIONS
2.2 STATISTICAL ISSUES AND DEFINITIONS (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes remote viewing and anomalous cognition experiments at SRI and SAIC: free-response vs. forced-choice designs, sender/monitor roles, and difficulty distinguishing telepathy, clairvoyance, and precognition. Argues that replicability in the long run, not on demand, is the standard, as with baseball hitting. Explains p-values, statistical significance at the 5 percent level, and why chance must be ruled out before accepting results.

nodes.title: replication
nodes.summary: Explains that replication success should be judged by effect size and magnitude rather than p-values, since small replications of large effects can fail statistical significance despite matching results. Uses a sex-determination example (70% boys in 100 births vs. 7 of 10) to illustrate. Notes conventional effect size benchmarks (0.2 small, 0.5 medium) and that the report focuses on the measure most used in remote viewing research at SRI and SAIC.

nodes.title: 2.2.2 REPLICATION AND EFFECT SIZES: In the past few decades scientists have
nodes.summary: Explains that statistical significance (p-values) should assess overall evidence, while replication success should be judged by achieving the original effect size or a stronger effect, not by p-value thresholds. Illustrates with a 70-percent-boys sex-determination example where a 10-birth replication is non-significant despite matching rate. Defines effect sizes (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large). Describes rank-order judging in remote viewing experiments: a random target selection from five candidates, blind judge ranks matches, and chance average rank is three.

nodes.title: 2.2.3 RANDOMNESS AND RANK-ORDER JUDGING.
nodes.summary: Explains rank-order judging for remote viewing experiments: a blind judge ranks one correct target against four decoys, chance average rank is three, and scores below three indicate anomalous cognition; the method is conservative and avoids ceiling effects. Converts average ranks to effect sizes (small 0.2, medium 0.5, large 0.8; maximum 1.4), and notes that randomness must be defined by target selection. Also covers methodological issues: early SRI experiments had information-leak loopholes, while later SRI and SAIC work was more rigorous, with exceptions in Appendix 2.

Describes SRI and SAIC remote viewing and anomalous cognition experiments, contrasting free-response and forced-choice designs and the difficulty of separating telepathy, clairvoyance, and precognition. Argues long-run replicability is the standard and covers p-values and the 5 percent significance threshold. Recommends judging replication by effect size rather than p-values, with benchmarks of 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. Explains rank-order judging: chance average rank is three, scores below three indicate anomalous cognition, and maximum effect size is 1.4. Notes early SRI experiments had information-leak loopholes, later work was more rigorous, and exceptions appear in Appendix 2.

nodes.title: 2.3 METHODOLOGICAL ISSUES
nodes.summary: Excerpt from an AIR review (Dr. Jessica Utts) of remote viewing research. Covers methodological safeguards for experiments: isolating viewers, judges, and targets from knowledge of targets; randomized target/decoy selection; duplicate target sets; pre-defined stopping rules and data exclusion criteria; pre-planned statistical analysis. Discusses rank-order scoring with five choices and effect sizes. Argues applied remote viewing anecdotes (May 1995) can be prima facie evidence when information was not normally attainable, while anecdotal psychic reports are weak proof.

nodes.title: 3.1 EARLY OPERATIONAL SUCCESSES AND EVALUATION
nodes.summary: Describes SRI remote viewing research from Puthoff and Targ (1975). Covers three reported operational successes (West Virginia site with underground facility and leaked codewords, Urals Communist Bloc site, Semipalatinsk site with a large gantry crane), verified as substantially correct by the sponsor. Notes evaluation problems: no baseline, differing evaluator expectations, possible subject contact with insiders, and selective report choice. Introduces the early controlled SRI experiments of 1974-1975, criticized on statistical and methodological grounds.

nodes.title: 3.2 THE EARLY SCIENTIFIC EFFORT AT SRI
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a CIA-declassified review of remote viewing research (SRI, 1973-1983). Covers a crane/gantry site operational test at Semipalatinsk, USSR, and how its evaluation was disputed due to lack of controls and selective reporting. Describes early 1974-75 controlled experiments with varied targets and criticisms of them, notably Dr. Jessica Utts's review of a 100-site series using sampling without replacement, where cues leaked between sessions. Summarizes a 1988 overall analysis of 154 SRI experiments (about 26,000 trials, 227 subjects) with results p<10^-14, which the authors say needs explanation beyond chance, though methodological flaws in earlier work remain a concern.

nodes.title: 3.3 AN OVERALL ANALYSIS OF THE SRI EXPERIMENTS: 1973-1983
nodes.summary: Summarizes an SRI remote viewing review by Dr. Jessica Utts: 1973-75 remote viewing series with 100 sites selected without replacement, eight viewers, and blind judging. Critics raised issues (site selection, cueing from transcripts, scoring). A 1988 overall analysis of 154 SRI experiments (1973-1983, about 26,000 trials, 227 subjects) gave p<10^-6, with a talented subgroup and free-response results stronger than forced choice. Findings: replicability, a small group of consistently successful viewers, feedback helps, training doesn't clearly improve ability, distance and electromagnetic shielding don't inhibit performance, precognition evidence is compelling, no evidence for psychokinesis. Effect sizes match other labs (PRL ganzfeld, 0.17 vs SRI 0.164 for novices), supporting validity.

nodes.title: 3.4 CONSISTENCY WITH OTHER LABORATORIES IN THE SAME ERA
nodes.summary: A declassified SRI remote viewing review (Dr. Jessica Utts) finds: distance and electromagnetic shielding do not impede performance; compelling evidence for precognition; no evidence for psychokinesis. Results are consistent with other labs: forced-choice precognition effect sizes (SRI 0.033 vs. 0.052 elsewhere, though methods differ), and ganzfeld studies (Princeton PRL 0.17, SRI 0.164; novices 0.35 vs. experienced 0.385), arguing against fraud or methodological flaws.

Describes ESP types (telepathy, clairvoyance, precognition, psychokinesis) and SRI/SAIC remote viewing research, contrasting free-response and forced-choice designs. Covers statistics: replicability, p-values at 5 percent, effect-size benchmarks (0.2/0.5/0.8), rank-order judging (chance rank three, maximum effect 1.4). Addresses methodological safeguards (isolation, randomized targets, pre-set stopping rules), early loophole-prone experiments, and operational successes lacking controls. Reviews the 1973-1983 SRI series (154 experiments, about 26,000 trials, 227 subjects, p<10^-6 to 10^-14): viewer consistency, feedback helps, training and distance/shielding have no clear effect, precognition compelling, no psychokinesis evidence. Effect sizes match other labs (ganzfeld, Princeton PRL 0.17 vs SRI 0.164), arguing against fraud.

nodes.title: 4. THE SAIC ERA
4. THE SAIC ERA (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a CIA-released American Institutes for Research review of SAIC (Science Applications International Corporation) psychic-research experiments, overseen by a Scientific Oversight Committee and reviewed via Dr. Edwin May's July 1995 memo. It lists ten experiments (six remote viewing, four other), with titles, trials, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and p-values, notes that Dr. Jessica Utts is Review 1, and explains that remote-viewing results are broken into homogeneous session sets (e.g., pilot E6 viewers at home with sealed envelopes), with trial-weighted overall effect sizes described in Appendix 2.

nodes.title: 4.3 ASSESSING THE REMOTE VIEWING EXPERIMENTS BY HOMOGENEOUS SETS OF SESSIONS
nodes.summary: Assesses SRI and remote viewing experiments by homogeneous session sets: Table 2 lists individual effect sizes by viewer and experiment (static vs. dynamic targets, expert viewers, notes on E4-E6). Discusses replicability: viewers 009 and 372 had similar effect sizes across SRI and SAIC (about .35-.385), with a .901 correlation across experiments. Static and dynamic target results diverged (p=.0073 vs p=.50), prompting a methodological investigation despite random target assignment.

nodes.title: 4.5 METHODOLOGICAL ISSUES IN THE REMOTE VIEWING EXPERIMENTS AT
nodes.summary: Methodological issues in SAIC remote viewing experiments (Section 4.5): viewers worked from homes and faxed responses to Dr. Lantz, who mailed answers; originals went to SAIC, with checks for tampering. Isolation rules kept viewers, target knowledge, and judges separated until responses were secured. Targets and decoys were randomly selected, with duplicate sets used for judging. Stopping rules and exclusion criteria should be predefined. Dr. Utts's review covers 40 trials per viewer across four conditions, with no aborted sessions, and calls for pre-planned analyses.

nodes.title: 4.6 WAS ANYTHING LEARNED AT SAIC?
key_items: 4.6.1 TARGET SELECTION. In addition to the question of whether or not psychic
nodes.summary: The text covers CIA-SAIC remote viewing research: Experiments 1 and 10 found a link between change in target visual entropy and remote viewing quality, replicated and not explained by artifacts; speculation on precognition and a 'psychic sense' analogous to change detection; the 'target pool bandwidth' hypothesis; Experiment 7 on remote staring (physiological influence between people), and Experiment 2 on enhanced binary computer guessing (51.6% vs 50%). It also reviews ganzfeld telepathy replications from PRL, Amsterdam, and Edinburgh, with hit rates of 32.2%, 37%, and 33% versus 25% chance.

nodes.title: 5.2 GANZFELD RESULTS FROM FOUR LABORATORIES
nodes.summary: Describes ganzfeld telepathy experiments replicated across four laboratories (PRL, University of Amsterdam, University of Edinburgh, Institute for Parapsychology NC) with hit rates of roughly 32-37 percent versus 25 percent chance, including Bem and Honorton's analysis excluding methodologically flawed studies (p=.002) and Morris et al.'s sender-condition results. Table 3 compares ganzfeld effect sizes (Cohen's h) with SRI and SAIC remote viewing results, showing sessions, hit rates, and effect sizes.

nodes.title: 5.3 CONCLUSIONS ABOUT EXTERNAL REPLICATION
nodes.summary: Conclusions on external replication: remote viewing effects have been conceptually replicated across labs and cultures, with consistent results unlikely due to methodological flaws. On usefulness: anomalous cognition may work for some people, with certain individuals (e.g., Viewer 372 at SAIC) better at specific tasks; end users must learn its scope; it is rarely 100% accurate with no reliable way to tell accurate from inaccurate output; and information useless for one purpose may help others, such as describing a hostage's location.

Excerpt from a CIA-released AIR review of SAIC psychic-research experiments (ten experiments, six remote viewing, with trials, effect sizes, CIs, p-values; Dr. Utts as Review 1). Covers homogeneous session sets and replicability across SRI and SAIC (viewers 009 and 372; static vs. dynamic target divergence), methodological issues (isolation, randomization, predefined stopping rules), SAIC findings (entropy-change link, remote staring, binary guessing) and ganzfeld replications across four labs, concluding remote viewing effects replicated but are inconsistent in accuracy and usefulness.

nodes.title: 7. CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
nodes.summary: Review 1 by Dr. Jessica Utts concludes anomalous cognition is possible and replicated across labs and cultures, based on accepted scientific criteria, not belief. Fraud or methodological flaws would need varied explanations, which no one has shown. Senders seem unnecessary and distance/time don't impede it. Mechanism remains unclear. Resources should target specific questions; answers are expected within a decade. Document is from American Institutes for Research, with OCR noise.

nodes.title: 8. REFERENCES
nodes.summary: A CIA-released (2002) research review chapter's reference list of parapsychology studies on anomalous cognition and the ganzfeld procedure. Cited works include Bem & Honorton (1994) on replicable evidence for anomalous information transfer; Bierman (1995) on the Amsterdam ganzfeld series; Broughton & Alexander (1995) on Autoganzfeld I; May et al. on feedback, target entropy, and SRI psychoenergetic research (1973-1988); May (1995) on AC technical trials; and Morris et al. (1995) on sender/no-sender conditions. Also Puthoff & Targ (1975) on perceptual augmentation techniques.

nodes.title: APPENDIX 1
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a declassified CIA document (Approved for Release 2002/05/22, RDP96-00791R000200180006-4), Review 1 by Dr. Jessica Utts, Appendix 1 on effect size measure for rank-order judging. Defines effect size as standard deviations between the true population value and chance-expected value, with the standard error used in the test. For rank-order judging with N choices, E(R)=(N+1)/2 and Var(R)=(N^2-1)/12; for N=5, E(R)=3 and Var(R)=2. Remaining text is OCR noise.

nodes.title: APPENDIX 2
A BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE SAIC EXPERIMENTS
EXPERIMENT 1: TARGET AND SENDER DEPENDENCIES:
nodes.summary: Describes SAIC Experiment 1 on remote viewing, testing whether a sender is needed and whether dynamic video-clip targets outperform static National Geographic photos. Five experienced viewers, 10 trials per condition, rank-order judging by a blinded analyst. No sender effect; static targets showed a moderate effect (ES .248, p=.0073), dynamic none. Speculated dynamic targets were too broad, leading to Experiment 10.

nodes.title: EXPERIMENT 4: ENHANCING DETECTION OF AC WITH BINARY CODING:
nodes.summary: Experiment 4 tested whether remote viewing could send messages by encoding five binary features (presence/absence) of targets as 2-bit numbers plus error-correction bits. Five viewers, eight targets, no sender, a week-long fixed-location protocol, and blind judging at SAIC were used. Neither rank-order judging nor binary-guess analysis showed any evidence of psychic functioning or a workable message-sending method.

nodes.title: EXPERIMENT 5: AC IN LUCID DREAMS (BASELINE):
nodes.summary: Describes Experiment 5, a baseline test (despite its name, not about lucid dreams) of three novice remote viewers doing standard lab remote viewing. Each completed eight trials using random National Geographic targets from SRI/SAIC sets, judged blind against four decoys by rank-ordering. One viewer had a promising but non-significant effect size of .265 due to few trials; the group effect size was 0.088, with no individual data for the other two.

nodes.title: EXPERIMENT 6: AC IN LUCID DREAMS (PILOT):
nodes.summary: Describes CIA-affiliated remote viewing experiments. Experiment 6 tests remote viewing during lucid dreams with seven viewers (four SAIC, three Lucidity Institute), 21 trials, viewers taking sealed NatGeo targets home, results blind-judged (p=.046, effect size 0.368). Experiment 9 tests EEG brainwave changes during remote viewing with three viewers (18, 24, 28 trials), noting the unfixed trial counts as a protocol weakness.

nodes.title: EXPERIMENT 9: ERD AC BEHAVIOR:
nodes.summary: Review of remote viewing experiments. Experiment 8: seven viewers, 21 trials total, unsealed targets taken home, blind-judged by sum-of-ranks, majority hits (p=.046), overall effect size 0.368; no novice/expert distinction given. Experiment 9: EEG measured during remote viewing by three experienced viewers (18, 24, 28 trials), effect sizes 0.432, 0.354, 0.177 (p=.033, .042, .175), overall 0.303 (p=.006); flagged protocol issue with unspecified trial counts.

nodes.title: EXPERIMENT 10: ENTROPY II:
nodes.summary: Describes Experiment 10 (Entropy II), an improved follow-up to Experiment 1 testing whether remote viewing success correlates with change in visual entropy of dynamic versus static targets, using a National Geographic-sized target pool. Four SAIC viewers (#009, 372, 389, S518) each did equal sessions; results show combined effect size .55 and z-score 5.22, with per-viewer tables. Also briefly covers four other SAIC experiments (MEG and EEG brain-signal tests, two replications) and Experiment 2, a sequential-analysis binary guessing test where subject 531 scored 76/100 (effect size .52, z 5.20) while others were at chance.

nodes.title: EXPERIMENT 2: AC OF BINARY TARGETS:
nodes.summary: Describes SAIC/SRI Experiment 2 testing whether humans can guess computer-selected binary (0/1) targets using sequential analysis. Subject 531 scored 76/100 (effect size .520, z=5.20), while subjects 007 and 083 showed chance results (44 and 49 correct). Required 21,337 guesses, so the method is inefficient. Combined results: 56% of 301 decisions correct, effect size 0.123, p=0.017, and a z-score of 4.65 for the combined data. Includes a Dr. Jessica Utts review.

nodes.title: EXPERIMENT 7: REMOTE OBSERVATION:
nodes.summary: Describes SAIC Experiment 7 on remote observation: whether a person's galvanic skin response rises when remotely watched. A observee was video-monitored while an observer in a distant room tried to influence physiology during randomly timed 30-second 'influence' periods versus control periods. Skin response was higher during watched periods in both experiments (p=.036 and .014; combined effect size .39), with a stronger effect for opposite-sex pairs. The discussion raises mechanism questions and calls for further study. Also includes review headers by Jessica Utts and Ray Hyman.

Summarizes SAIC remote viewing experiments 1-10 and related tests. Exp 1: sender and target dependencies, static targets showed a modest effect. Exp 2: binary-target guessing via sequential analysis; subject 531 scored 76/100, combined z=4.65. Exp 4: binary-coded messaging, no evidence. Exp 5: novice baseline, group effect 0.088. Exp 6: lucid-dream pilot, p=.046. Exp 7: remote observation raised skin response (combined ES .39). Exp 8/9: viewer study and EEG tests, overall ES .303. Exp 10 (Entropy II): combined ES .55, z=5.22. Includes reviews by Utts and Hyman.

nodes.title: INTRODUCTION
nodes.summary: The text introduces a review of the SRI and SAIC 'Anomalous Mental Phenomena' (psi) program, 1973-1994, evaluating Professor Jessica Utts's claims of anomalous cognition (clairvoyance, precognition) and finding no evidence for anomalous perturbation. It focuses on the 10 SAIC experiments, notes methodological flaws in earlier SRI remote viewing work, and says both reviewers agree SAIC experiments are free of obvious flaws and effect sizes are large and consistent. They disagree on whether the effects establish anomalous cognition, whether flaws are eliminated, and whether SAIC results match other labs. It closes by stressing that science requires independent replication.

nodes.title: SCIENTIFIC STATUS OF THE PROGRAM
nodes.summary: Covers a review of the SAIC/SRI psi research program's scientific status. Key disagreements: whether non-chance effects establish anomalous cognition, whether methodological flaws are eliminated, and whether SAIC results match other remote viewing and ganzfeld labs. Argues science requires independent replication and peer review. Notes the program ran over twenty years but produced only about ten adequate experiments from one lab, spreading inquiry too thin under sponsor-driven secrecy, so scientific contribution is limited.

nodes.title: GENERAL SCIENTIFIC HANDICAPS OF THE SAIC PROGRAM
nodes.summary: Review by Dr. Ray Hyman of the SAIC/SRI psi research program: argues the program lacked normal scientific checks (secrecy, no peer review or replication), spread too few experiments (about ten) across too many questions, and produced no reliable results. Also traces parapsychology's quest for scientific status from the 1882 Society for Psychical Research through Rhine's 1930s statistical work, the replication failures, and the cheating scandals that hurt its acceptance.

nodes.title: PARAPSYCHOLOGY’S STATUS AS A SCIENCE
nodes.summary: An excerpt from an American Institutes for Research review (Review 2 by Dr. Ray Hyman) assessing the scientific status of parapsychology and the SAIC remote viewing program. It covers the field's history from the 1882 Society for Psychical Research, J.B. Rhine's 1930s statistical work and criticism, and the replicability problem, including Pratt's and Honorton's positions and Jessica Utts's meta-analytic claim of replicated anomalous effects. Hyman argues effect-size consistency does not prove anomalous phenomena. He contends parapsychology lacks a cumulative database, since past evidence (Creery sisters, Smith-Blackburn, Rhine cards, Soal-Goldney, Sheep-Goats) was discarded, and warns that current ganzfeld and remote viewing evidence may suffer the same fate. He concludes that the science status remains shaky.

nodes.title: THE CLAIM THAT ANOMALOUS COGNITION EXISTS
nodes.summary: Critiques Professor Jessica Utts' claim that psychic functioning is established, based on three premises: parapsychological statistical results are far beyond chance, methodological flaws are refuted, and effects replicated across labs. Explains that parapsychology uniquely relies on chance-departure statistics, unlike other sciences that began with directly observable phenomena. Argues statistical significance alone cannot prove anomalous cognition because models are idealized and significance can arise from many mundane causes. Discusses how absence of flaws can never be fully guaranteed, citing historical cases (Soal-Goldney fraud, ganzfeld flaws, Bem and Honorton's flawed randomization) and the need for debugging new protocols. Notes averaged effect sizes are misleading due to unequal contributions and heterogeneity. Introduces SAIC experiments as improved but with possible remaining issues such as repeated viewers and targets.

nodes.title: THE SAIC PROGRAM
nodes.summary: Excerpts from a CIA-released review of SRI/SAIC remote viewing parapsychology experiments. Covers: meaninglessness of averaging effect sizes across heterogeneous studies dominated by one experimenter; static vs. dynamic target results; SAIC improvements in randomization and independence alongside problems of repeated viewers, targets, investigators, and a single principal judge; critique of secrecy and lack of independent replication; and argument that anomalous cognition is unproven, requiring replication with new viewers, targets, independent judges, and independent labs to rule out mundane explanations.

nodes.title: HAS ANOMALOUS COGNITION BEEN PROVEN?
nodes.summary: Critique of parapsychology research (Review 2 by Dr. Ray Hyman) arguing that anomalous cognition has not been proven. It covers the need for a positive theory specifying when psi is present, the decline effect and its misuse as a psi token, displacement effects and other post-hoc 'hidden signs,' and the problem of consistency claims. It discusses ganzfeld experiments (introversion/extroversion, static vs. dynamic targets, bandwidth explanations), the lack of an own-judge vs. external-judge pattern, and the requirements for compelling evidence: replication by independent labs, new viewers and judges, and ruling out artifacts.

nodes.title: WHAT NEEDS TO BE EXPLAINED?
WHAT NEEDS TO BE EXPLAINED? (intro)
nodes.summary: Review 2 by Dr. Ray Hyman critiques parapsychology research, specifically the SAIC remote viewing and ganzfeld experiments that Professor Utts cites as evidence of anomalous cognition. Hyman argues that statistical significance alone cannot establish an anomaly: null-hypothesis rejection is an approximation, sufficient power guarantees significance even for trivial effects, and parapsychology lacks the reliable exemplar experiments found in other sciences (e.g., Ebbinghaus, Newton). He cites the mitogenetic radiation, N-rays, and polywater failures, and contrasts parapsychology's vague 'anomaly' with Leverrier's precisely specified Uranus discrepancy that led to Neptune's discovery. Hyman concedes significant effects exist but finds no obvious methodological flaws explaining them, notes possible biases such as single judges and experimenter coaching, and says the results lack lawful, specifiable conditions, so the field is not yet ready for scientific acceptance.

nodes.title: POTENTIALS FOR OPERATIONAL APPLICATIONS
nodes.summary: The text, from an American Institutes for Research review of parapsychology, asks whether remote viewing has operational intelligence value. Even if real, its accuracy is only partly correct (about 20% per Ed May) with no way to tell which parts, and it is unclear when it works. Parapsychology relies on markers like the decline effect and hitting variability, which cannot distinguish presence from absence of psi. Subjective validation drives operational claims, as shown by Marks and Kammann's experience and Ray Hyman's critique, where judges matched protocols to the wrong targets. Double-blind tests with decoy targets are recommended. The SAIC and ganzfeld experiments are methodologically strong, but the case for anomalous cognition remains shaky.

Section 'What needs to be explained?' covers Ray Hyman's critique of parapsychology (SAIC remote viewing and ganzfeld experiments cited by Utts): statistical significance alone cannot establish anomaly, power yields significance for trivial effects, and the field lacks reliable exemplar experiments, citing N-rays, polywater, and mitogenetic radiation; Hyman concedes significant effects but finds no obvious methodological flaws, notes possible biases, and says lawful conditions are absent. The second part, from an AIR review, questions remote viewing's operational value: accuracy is partial and unidentifiable, markers like decline effect cannot separate psi from chance, subjective validation drives claims, and double-blind decoy tests are recommended.

nodes.title: SUGGESTIONS: WHAT NEXT?
SUGGESTIONS: WHAT NEXT? (intro)
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a CIA-released review of SAIC remote viewing experiments. Covers: the double-blind protocol where judges matched verbal descriptions to actual versus decoy targets; concern that suggestive interrogation and sensory cues could explain matches; the view that matches to true targets would be evidence for remote viewing; and skepticism (Dr. Ray Hyman) that significant results prove anomalous cognition given design flaws. Recommends independent replication with new viewers, judges, labs and targets, and developing a positive theory of anomalous communication.

nodes.title: CONCLUSIONS
nodes.summary: Conclusions from a review of SAIC remote viewing research on anomalous mental phenomena. Hyman argues the experiments were methodologically superior to earlier SRI work, but secrecy and too many demands left the program scientifically underdeveloped, with no finding followed up in enough detail. Statistical departures from chance may reflect flaws or real effects, yet they don't prove anomalous cognition; results are preliminary, and the field needs replication by independent judges and labs, with specified boundary conditions. Operational claims are hazardous due to subjective validation. Utts replies that parapsychology has a cumulative database, builds on past work like normal science, and that its effects are statistical, like aspirin-heart attack links, requiring large samples.

Section on SAIC remote viewing experiments reviewed for a CIA release. Covers the double-blind judging protocol and concerns that interrogation cues could explain matches; skepticism from Ray Hyman that significant results don't prove anomalous cognition due to design flaws. Recommends independent replication with new viewers, judges, labs, and targets, plus a positive theory of anomalous communication. Conclusions: experiments were methodologically better than earlier SRI work but scientifically underdeveloped due to secrecy; deviations from chance are preliminary, not proof; operational claims are hazardous. Utts replies that parapsychology builds cumulatively like normal science, with small statistical effects requiring large samples.

Appendix 2 covers a review of SRI/SAIC remote viewing psi experiments (1973-1994), including SAIC Experiments 1-10 with mixed effect sizes (e.g., Exp 10 combined ES .55, z=5.22) and Utts's claims of anomalous cognition. Ray Hyman critiques the program's secrecy, lack of replication, small number of adequate experiments, and heterogeneous meta-analytic averaging, and questions whether effects prove anomalous cognition or operational value. Discussion covers parapsychology's history, past discarded evidence, methodological flaws, needed replications with new viewers, judges and labs, and Utts's cumulative-science reply.

nodes.title: Discussion
nodes.summary: A CIA-released review (American Institutes for Research) of remote viewing research summarizes expert reviewers Dr. Jessica Utts and Dr. Ray Hyman. They agree that laboratory studies show a statistically significant effect and that methodology has improved, but disagree on causation: Utts favors a paranormal explanation while Hyman says competing explanations and criterion contamination remain unruled out. Concerns include repeated use of the same viewers, judges, targets, and scoring, which risks monomethod bias, and the need for independent replication. They also disagree on whether the effect is consistent enough to be useful. Conclusions: a statistical anomaly exists, but paranormal ability is not demonstrated, mechanisms are unidentified, and there is no evidence of intelligence-gathering utility.

nodes.title: The fourth and final question presented
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a CIA-released American Institutes for Research review of remote viewing (psychic spying) research. Covers panel reviewers' disagreement (Utts favorable, Hyman skeptical) and four questions: whether direct evidence of paranormal ability exists, whether the research program identified mechanisms, whether it is adequate and replicable, and whether it supports intelligence gathering. Conclusions: a statistically significant anomaly was found, but no convincing demonstration of paranormal ability, no identified source, and no evidence of intelligence utility. Also includes Utts's reply and the start of Chapter Four on evaluating remote viewing's utility for intelligence operations, including boundary conditions research.

key_items: Senders and Distance. When one considers the remote viewing paradigm, one
nodes.summary: The text is a chapter from an RAND/American Institutes for Research report evaluating the operational utility of remote viewing for intelligence. It reviews boundary conditions: sender and distance requirements, static versus dynamic targets, information specificity and judging via binary coding, feedback needs, viewer training and rarity of talent, and inter-judge agreement and cueing effects. It concludes laboratory evidence does not justify operational use. It then introduces interviews with program users, remote viewers, and the Program Manager, with details in Appendix C.

nodes.title: Interview Findings
Interview Findings (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes an operational evaluation of remote viewing for intelligence use. Laboratory studies give a foundation but their findings argue against operational use due to target types, lack of feedback, inconsistent accuracy, and unexamined boundary conditions. Structured interviews with recent users, remote viewers, and the Program Manager found users tried viewings exploratorily, targets were operational rather than lab-like, reports were 3-4 pages with drawings and verbal descriptions, and information was often vague.

nodes.title: C) , initial interest in the
nodes.summary: A CIA-released chapter on evaluating remote viewing utility in intelligence operations. Covers interview questions written with the program, end-user interviews on accuracy and operational value, and users' exploratory use when traditional options were exhausted. Tasks included identifying people, objects, and locations, typically with three independent viewings summarized in 3-4 page reports. Five general observations: information was stated in broad, vague terms, and reports were most likely accurate only with respect to general, stereotypical features of the situation.

nodes.title: characteristics
characteristics (intro)
nodes.summary: Remote viewing program evaluation (CIA-era, Chapter Four). Viewings were judged inaccurate, inconsistent, and too nonspecific to serve as primary intelligence, so they were used only as supplemental background, mainly when other sources were unavailable. Viewers' reports were sometimes altered by managers to fit known facts. Users were unwilling to fund viewings, partly due to cost and controversy. Viewers said requested information types did not suit remote viewing, and that outcomes depended on user engagement. The program manager noted limited operational use, suggested declassifying the research, and proposed contracting out the service.

nodes.title: Conclusions
nodes.summary: Conclusions from CIA-era remote viewing evaluation: interviews covered only recent operations, and findings are qualitative. Viewing information is vague, general, inconsistent across viewings, lacks specific content matching known facts, and includes much irrelevant or erroneous material, placing the sorting burden on users and risking misallocated resources. Accuracy seems limited to broad background that good analysis could produce. Acceptance is controversial and existing lab research gives little support. Conclusion: the program has limited operational value; specific, reliable, verifiable research is needed.

nodes.title: User Assessments
nodes.summary: Declassified CIA-era evaluation of remote viewing for intelligence use, based on 1994-1995 user assessments of 40 viewings rated on accuracy (six-point scale, average 3.0) and value (five-point scale, average 3.5), showing low value. Results were better for broad background than for concrete, actionable information, with accuracy tied to available background data. No individual viewer stood out, and tasks from people-tracking versus combat organizations differed. Concludes remote viewing has limited to no real value for intelligence gathering, with further work hard to justify.

Evaluation of CIA-era remote viewing found viewings inaccurate, inconsistent, and nonspecific, so used only as supplemental background. Managers sometimes altered reports; users were unwilling to fund it due to cost and controversy; viewers said requests were ill-suited. The program had limited operational use, was proposed for declassification and contracting out. Conclusions: vague, mostly irrelevant output with little lab support, so limited value. 1994-1995 ratings of 40 viewings were low (accuracy 3.0/6, value 3.5/5), better for broad background, with no standout viewer, so further work is hard to justify.

An operational evaluation of remote viewing for intelligence use finds lab studies argue against operational use: wrong target types, no feedback, inconsistent accuracy, untested boundaries. Interviews with users, viewers, and the Program Manager show exploratory use, operational targets, vague 3-4 page reports, and three viewings per task. Observations: outputs were broad, mostly accurate only on stereotypical features. Program was judged of limited value, costly, controversial; 1994-95 ratings were low (accuracy 3.0/6, value 3.5/5).

Fragmentary OCR from a CIA-released American Institutes for Research review of remote viewing research (Chapter Three). Panel reviewers Jessica Utts (favorable, paranormal explanation) and Ray Hyman (skeptical, alternative explanations and criterion contamination) agree on a significant laboratory effect and improved methodology but disagree on causation, consistency, and replication. Concerns include monomethod bias from repeated viewers, judges, targets, and scoring. Conclusions: a statistical anomaly exists, but paranormal ability, mechanisms, and intelligence utility are unshown. Chapter Four covers boundary conditions and interviews: lab evidence does not justify operational use; users found outputs vague, mostly accurate only on stereotypical features, costly, and of limited value (1994-95 ratings: accuracy 3.0/6, value 3.5/5).

summary: Chapter Three of a CIA-released American Institutes for Research report reviews two decades of government-sponsored remote viewing research at SRI and SAIC. Dr. Jessica Utts (favorable) and Dr. Ray Hyman (skeptical) review the evidence, with Utts's reply and points of agreement and disagreement. Findings: a replicated, statistically significant laboratory effect of small-to-medium size, but unproven causation, mechanism, consistency, and operational usefulness. Also covers methodology, meta-analysis, and references.

title: Chapter Five: Conclusions

nodes.title: Chapter Five: Conclusions (intro)
nodes.summary: The text is the concluding chapter of a CIA-released report evaluating remote viewing, a claimed paranormal phenomenon, and its potential use in intelligence gathering. It describes a structured, unbiased, multifaceted program evaluation covering the research effort and its applications, and states that the section summarizes conclusions drawn from evaluative data presented in preceding sections, with much evidence bearing on the phenomenon's existence and intelligence value.

nodes.title: Summary of Key Findings
nodes.summary: A review of remote viewing lab experiments by two reviewers (one sympathetic to paranormal claims, one skeptic) found a statistically significant effect but no unequivocal proof of a paranormal phenomenon. Key problems: only one judge (the Principal Investigator, familiar with viewers) was used, with no independent judges, and some reports were altered to match background cues. Remote viewing is unlikely to be useful for intelligence operations, which need concrete, actionable information, so continued operational support is not justified.

nodes.title: Appendix D: Star Gate Operational Tasking» Evaluation
1.0 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
nodes.summary: A CIA-released appendix evaluating the DoD Star Gate remote viewing program's operational tasking from 1986 to Q1 FY1995. Over 200 tasks were received; in 1994 DIA created a scoring method. By May 1995, 40 tasks from five organizations were answered. Accuracy scores clustered at 2-3 (13 scored 1); value scores clustered at 3-4 (none scored 1). Authors conclude RV's operational utility for intelligence cannot be substantiated, based on product evaluations and user interviews, and that its subjective nature creates analyst burden of questionable return.

nodes.title: 2.0 GENERIC DESCRIPTION OF OPERATIONAL TASKING
nodes.summary: Covers the Star Gate program's operational tasking from 1986 to Q1 FY1995: over 200 tasks from military organizations asked remote viewers to describe targets (people, places, vessels, North Korean tunnels, leadership intentions) with minimal specificity. Until 1994 results were unscored; a 1994 numerical evaluation method then scored 40 tasks from five organizations by May 1995. Describes the typical tasking workflow (PM tasking form, individual RV sessions, collected inputs, evaluator scoring), tasking-form example, and vague targets that allowed loose interpretation of accuracy and value.

nodes.title: 3.0 EVALUATION MEASURES
nodes.summary: Describes the CIA StarGate evaluation report (Appendix D). Covers DIAM 58-13 numeric scoring for Accuracy (Yes/May be true/Possible true/No/Possibly not true/Unsure) and Value (Major/High/Low/No value), with hedged modifiers making ratings subjective; 39 of 40 tasks evaluated in 1994-1995 across three remote viewers, with score averages, standard deviations, and histograms showing Accuracy clustering at 3-4 and Value at 2-3.

nodes.title: 4.0 EVALUATION SUMMARY AND COMMENTS
nodes.summary: Appendix D of a CIA-approved document on the Star Gate remote viewing program (American Institutes for Research) reviews operational user interviews. It defines intelligence value ratings (major, high, low, no value) from DIAM 58-13 and summarizes evaluation of 39 numerically scored remote viewing tasks from 1994-1995, covering Accuracy and Value scores by evaluator and tasking organization, with averages and standard deviations. It notes Value scores run lower than Accuracy, discusses suspect high Accuracy scores on publicized topics, and attributes scoring discrepancies among organizations (Org. A higher, Org. B above C, Org. E low) to evaluator bias and subjectivity. It also discusses telegraphing, knowledge bias, and the narrow information bandwidth that make evaluation difficult.

nodes.title: 5.0 GENERAL COMMENTS ON THE PROCESS
nodes.summary: The text is an OCR-garbled CIA document excerpt (Approved for Release 2002, Appendix D, StarGate operational interviews) covering general process comments: nonspecific, unstructured remote-viewing tasking; telegraphed information and evaluator bias making scoring subjective; accuracy necessary but not sufficient for utility; protocol inconsistencies; North Korea and Middle East tasking data; and summaries of user interviews finding users grasped at straws, outputs were never specific enough to act on or corroborate, and the service was not worth paying for.

nodes.title: 6.0 SUMMARY FROM USER INTERVIEWS (U)
nodes.summary: Appendix D of a CIA StarGate remote-viewing evaluation covers user interviews with tasking organizations. Users pursued the program out of hope for anything useful; outputs were never specific enough to task other assets or corroborate, though occasionally accurate in general terms. Org. C scored higher than Org. B, possibly due to belief differences, and Org. A's scoring may reflect a beacon-assist procedure and evaluator subjectivity. Conclusion: the information's value cannot be readily discerned; the process is subjective, adds analyst burden, and whether value justifies cost remains open.

nodes.title: 7.2 RECOMMENDATIONS
nodes.summary: Recommends applying scientific method to remote viewing (RV) parapsychology: validation may never meet scientific standards due to uncontrollable variables and lack of repeatable, independent results. Suggests clearer scoring definitions, multiple independent evaluators, and blind tests using known targets, while noting the field's controversy. Also discusses target specificity affecting accuracy (higher for North Korea tasks) and proposes post-analysis of precognitive predictions as a future study.

CIA-released Appendix D evaluates the DoD Star Gate remote viewing program's operational tasking (1986 to Q1 FY1995): over 200 tasks, 40 scored by May 1995 using a 1994 DIA method. Accuracy clustered at 2-3 and Value at 3-4; authors find RV's intelligence utility unsubstantiated, with subjective scoring adding analyst burden. Covers tasking workflow, DIAM 58-13 measures, evaluator bias, telegraphing, user interviews (outputs too vague to act on or corroborate), and recommendations for scientific validation, blind tests, and clearer scoring.

Appendices cover reviewer vitae (Hyman, Utts), SRI/SAIC bibliography, interviewer materials, Star Gate operational tasking evaluation (accuracy 2-3, value 3-4, vague unverifiable outputs), and user interviews finding results non-actionable.
